method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **A common, self-limiting viral skin infection of childhood.**
claims.source_text: Molluscum contagiosum virus (molluscum) is a common, self-limiting, viral infection of the skin … Molluscum is a common viral infection of childhood
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis is clinical, from the characteristic lesions; no investigations are needed.**
claims.source_text: Investigations are not required … The diagnosis of molluscum is made clinically by characteristic appearance of the lesions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with a central pit**, usually 1–3 mm but up to 1–2 cm.
claims.source_text: Firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication (pit) Lesions are usually 1-3mm in diameter, but can grow to 1-2cm
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Anywhere except the palms and soles**; commonest on the trunk, axillae, antecubital and popliteal fossae and groin. **Autoinoculation explains most anogenital lesions in children.**
claims.source_text: Lesions can occur anywhere on the body except the palms and soles, and a child may develop a few or many lesions … The most common areas include the trunk, axillae, antecubital and popliteal fossae and groin. Autoinoculation is responsible for most anogenital lesions in children
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Spread is by skin-to-skin contact, fomites (eg towels) or autoinoculation** by scratching or touching a lesion.
claims.source_text: Molluscum is spread by direct skin-to-skin contact, fomites (eg towel) or auto-inoculation by scratching or touching a lesion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eczema raises the risk of molluscum, and molluscum worsens the surrounding eczema** — children with eczema may have more extensive, longer-lasting lesions. **Optimise eczema management.**
claims.source_text: Eczema increases the risk of molluscum infection which in turn can exacerbate eczema in the surrounding skin. Optimise eczema management … Children with pre-existing eczema may have more extensive and longer lasting molluscum
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eczema can hide the primary lesions**; a careful history of how the first lesions looked is usually diagnostic.
claims.source_text: Recognition of molluscum can be difficult as eczema can obliterate the primary lesions, however a carefully taken history about the appearance of the initial lesions is usually diagnostic
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most cases clear in 6–9 months, but lesions can persist over a year**; full resolution needs an immune response, which may take 3 months to 3 years.
claims.source_text: Most cases resolve spontaneously within 6-9 months, but lesions can persist for more than a year … Complete resolution will happen when an immune response develops, which may take from 3 months to 3 years
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No exclusion from day care or school**, and no isolation or activity restriction. **Avoid sharing towels and bathing together** to protect siblings.
claims.source_text: Exclusion from day care or school is not required Children with molluscum should not be isolated or restricted in their activities Avoid sharing towels and bathing together to reduce the risk of spread to siblings
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most children need no treatment.** Consider it if quality of life is affected or the child is immunocompromised.
claims.source_text: Most children do not require treatment Treatment is considered if affecting quality of life or immunocompromised
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Cryotherapy and curettage are not routinely recommended in children** — they may scar. **Refer to dermatology for cantharidin**, a topical blistering agent that should not scar when used appropriately.
claims.source_text: Physical treatments such as cryotherapy or curettage are not routinely recommended for children and may cause scarring … Refer to specialist dermatology services for consideration of cantharidin treatment, a topical blistering agent which when used appropriately should not cause scarring
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Inflamed lesions often need no antibiotics**; consider them for purulent exudate, abscess or extending erythema.
claims.source_text: Lesions can become inflamed but antibiotic treatment is often not needed (consider antibiotics if purulent exudate, abscess or extending erythema)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the local paediatric team** if the diagnosis is uncertain or eczema is severe.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when the diagnosis is uncertain severe eczema
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Molluscum contagiosum' (Last updated March 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Molluscum_contagiosum/, retrieved 2026-09-23
